summary.text: Precipitation is water vapor that has condensed and falls from clouds under gravity, as drizzle, rain, sleet, snow, ice pellets, graupel or hail.
It falls once cloud particles grow too heavy for moving air to hold them up, which is why fog and mist, which do not fall, are not precipitation.
Precipitation deposits most of the planet's fresh water, about 505,000 cubic kilometres a year, most of it over the oceans.

items.prompt: Thick fog hangs in a valley all morning, soaking everything it touches. Why doesn't it count as precipitation?

options.label: It contains no liquid water at all
Its water stays suspended instead of falling
It is too warm to count as weather
It only forms over lakes and rivers

items.explain: Precipitation must fall; fog's water vapor does not condense enough to precipitate, so fog does not fall.

items.prompt: Where on Earth does most precipitation fall?
items.explain: Most precipitation occurs within the tropics, driven by convection.

items.prompt: Moist wind blows steadily up one side of a tall mountain range and down the other. Where are you most likely to find a desert?

options.label: On the slopes facing the wind

items.explain: Rising air on the windward side can bring heavy precipitation, while the leeward side gets dry air from compressional heating.

items.prompt: Raindrops land on cold cars and power lines and turn to ice the instant they touch. What is this called?
items.explain: Rain that freezes on contact in subfreezing air is freezing rain; hail, graupel and ice pellets are already frozen as they fall.

items.prompt: A storm drops 10 mm of rain. How much water landed on each square metre of ground?
items.explain: One millimetre of rain equals one litre per square metre, so 10 mm is 10 litres on each square metre.

items.prompt: A sudden summer downpour soaks the street in minutes, while a grey day brings only light rain. What drives the downpour?

options.label: A layer of fog becoming heavier
Strong vertical motion in the air

items.explain: Convective processes involve strong vertical motions and heavy precipitation, while stratiform processes have weaker upward motions and lighter precipitation.

pack.title: Why Clouds Finally Let Go
pack.question: What makes water in a cloud fall to the ground?

beats.title: Why Clouds Finally Let Go
beats.hook: Fog is made of water, yet it never counts as precipitation.

beats.prompt: Moist air is pushed up the windward side of a mountain range and spills down the other side. What is the far side likely to be like?
beats.explain: Upslope flow brings heavy precipitation to the windward side, while compressional heating leaves dry air, and sometimes desert, on the leeward side.

choices.label: Just as wet as the windward side
choices.feedback: It seems the same air should rain on both sides, but the air that descends is dry.

choices.label: Wetter than the windward side
choices.feedback: Heavy precipitation is on the windward side, where air flows uphill.

beats.prompt: Sort each type of precipitation by how it falls.
beats.explain: Rain and drizzle are liquid forms, while snow, hail, graupel and ice pellets fall as ice.

beats.prompt: Match each way of making precipitation to its description.

right.label: Air flowing up the windward side of mountains

beats.explain: Each mechanism differs in how the air is forced upward and how hard it rains.

beats.prompt: Put the steps that lead to rain in order.

items.label: Air becomes saturated by cooling or gaining water vapor
Vapor in the rising air condenses into clouds
Cloud droplets grow large enough to become raindrops

beats.explain: Air must first be saturated, then vapor condenses into cloud, and only once droplets are big enough do they fall.

beats.idea: Precipitation falls once cloud particles grow too heavy for moving air to hold up, reaching the ground as liquid, freezing liquid or ice.
